title: Boss: the container help desk
summary: Tickets from teammates whose containers misbehave, worked on a real Docker Engine.

steps.title: Your queue
body: You are the person the team asks when "Docker is broken". Most tickets come down to three things: the app is not
reachable, a container stopped (or keeps stopping), or two names are secretly the same image.
Each ticket below opens a terminal on its own machine with a **real Docker Engine** and the broken setup on it.
Investigate with `docker ps -a`, `docker logs`, `docker inspect` and `docker image ls`, then fix or answer.

steps.title: Ticket 1: "the API is up but I can't reach it"
prompt: A real Docker Engine runs in this terminal. A teammate started the API with
`docker run -d --name api -p 8080:80 shop/api:2.0`. `docker ps` says it is up, yet `curl http://localhost:8080/health`
Find out why, and leave a container named `api` from `shop/api:2.0` running so that
`curl http://localhost:8080/health` prints `ok`. (The app's own log says how to configure it.)

checks.name: it is a container named api from shop/api:2.0
checks.fail: There should be a running container `api` from `shop/api:2.0`.

hints: `docker logs api` shows the address and port the app really listens on.
Two problems: the published container port must be the one the app listens on, and an app listening on 127.0.0.1 *inside* the container cannot be reached from outside it.
`docker rm -f api`, then `docker run -d --name api -p 8080:8000 -e BIND=0.0.0.0 shop/api:2.0`.
steps.explain: "Up" only means the process runs. Reachability needs two things to line up: `-p HOST:CONTAINER` must point at the port the app really listens on, and the app must listen on `0.0.0.0` inside the container, because the container's own `127.0.0.1` is not the host's. The app's startup log line is the fastest way to see both.

steps.title: Ticket 2: "half the containers are weird"
prompt: A real Docker Engine runs in this terminal with six containers: `web`, `api`, `db`, `proxy`, `job` and `worker`.
Read their states (do not fix or remove anything), and answer with container names, one per line:
2. `~/answers/oom.txt`: the containers the kernel killed for using **too much memory**.

checks.name: unhealthy.txt is right
checks.fail: Not the right list. `docker ps --filter health=unhealthy` shows containers whose healthcheck fails.

checks.name: oom.txt is right
checks.cmd: diff <(for c in $(docker ps -aq); do docker inspect -f '{{.Name}} {{.State.OOMKilled}}' $c; done | awk '$2=="true"{print substr($1,2)}' | sort) <(sort -u ~/answers/oom.txt | sed '/^$/d')
checks.fail: Not the right list. Exit code 137 means SIGKILL, from the OOM killer **or** from anyone else: `docker inspect -f '{{.State.OOMKilled}}' NAME` tells them apart.

checks.name: looping.txt is right
checks.cmd: diff <(for c in $(docker ps -aq); do docker inspect -f '{{.Name}} {{.RestartCount}}' $c; done | awk '$2>0{print substr($1,2)}' | sort) <(sort -u ~/answers/looping.txt | sed '/^$/d')
checks.fail: Not the right list. A container in a restart loop shows `Restarting (1)` or a growing `{{.RestartCount}}` in `docker inspect`.

hints: `docker ps -a` shows `(unhealthy)`, `Restarting (...)` and `Exited (...)` in the STATUS column; `--filter health=unhealthy` and `--filter status=restarting` select them.
Two containers exited with 137. Only one of them was killed for memory: `docker inspect -f '{{.State.OOMKilled}}' db worker`.
`docker inspect -f '{{.Name}} {{.RestartCount}} {{.State.OOMKilled}}' $(docker ps -aq)` prints every container on one line each.
solution: docker inspect -f '{{.Name}} exit={{.State.ExitCode}} oom={{.State.OOMKilled}} restarts={{.RestartCount}}' $(docker ps -aq)
steps.explain: The STATUS column is a summary of `.State`: `docker inspect` has the facts behind it. Exit 137 is "killed by SIGKILL", and only `OOMKilled: true` says the kernel did it for memory; `worker` was killed by something else. A restart loop hides a crash behind `--restart always`: the restart count is the giveaway.

steps.title: Ticket 3: "are these the same image?"
prompt: A real Docker Engine runs in this terminal. The team has tagged the API image many times, and tried builds without `-t`; `docker image ls`
1. Write into `~/answers/same.txt` every name (`REPOSITORY:TAG`, one per line) that points at the **same image** as
2. The builds without `-t` left **untagged (dangling)** images behind. Remove them, and only them: every tagged image must stay.

checks.name: same.txt lists exactly the names of shop/api:1.4's image
checks.cmd: id=$(docker image inspect -f '{{.Id}}' shop/api:1.4); diff <(docker image ls --format '{{.Repository}}:{{.Tag}}' | while read r; do [ "$(docker image inspect -f '{{.Id}}' $r 2>/dev/null)" = "$id" ] && echo $r; done | sort) <(sort -u ~/answers/same.txt | sed '/^$/d')
checks.fail: Not the right list. Names that share an image ID are the same image: `docker image ls --format '{{.ID}} {{.Repository}}:{{.Tag}}'`.

checks.name: no dangling images are left
checks.fail: There are still untagged images. `docker image ls --filter dangling=true` lists them.

checks.name: every tagged image is still there
checks.cmd: for r in shop/api:1.4 shop/api:latest registry.example.com/shop/api:1.4 shop/api:1.5 shop/api:stable shop/api:dev alpine:3.24 busybox:1.37; do docker image inspect $r >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo missing $r; exit 1; }; done
checks.fail: A tagged image was removed. `docker image prune -a` also removes tagged images no container uses: plain `docker image prune` only removes dangling ones. Press Reset scenario.

hints: An image ID identifies the content; tags are names on top. `docker image ls --format '{{.ID}} {{.Repository}}:{{.Tag}}'`.
`docker image inspect -f '{{.Id}}' NAME` prints the full ID of one name, to compare.
`docker image prune -f` removes dangling images only; `-a` would remove unused tagged ones too.
steps.explain: Image IDs are content addresses: three names, one image, no extra disk. A build without `-t` (or an image whose tag moved on) leaves an untagged, dangling image behind, which is how a CI runner or dev laptop slowly fills up; `docker image prune` is the safe clean-up, and `-a` is the aggressive one that also removes tagged images no container uses.
